title: The Trivium
author: Davis C. Smith
summary: Davis C. Smith reviews Sister Miriam Joseph's The Trivium, a dense 1937 classroom text on grammar, logic, and rhetoric newly released to the public. Smith situates the book against a shift in the classical-education movement away from the developmental-stages reading of the Trivium (popularised by Dorothy Sayers) toward the language of wonder, leisure, and virtue, arguing that the seven liberal arts remain central rather than incidental to any education claiming continuity with the Western tradition. He highlights Joseph's distinctive ordering (logic first as the art of thinking, then grammar, then rhetoric) and her marriage of the Trivium to the literary tradition, while noting real shortcomings: no formal sentence analysis, an idiosyncratic shorthand for propositions, and a rhetoric section that is almost an afterthought. Smith concludes that the book is demanding but is perhaps the best available single-volume resource for the arts of language.
points: Smith frames the review against a movement-wide shift from utilitarian language (rigor, fluency, well-roundedness) toward wonder, leisure, contemplation, and virtue.
Joseph orders the arts unusually, placing logic first as the art of thinking, then grammar, then rhetoric, a progression that makes sense within her framework.
A major asset is Joseph's linking of the Trivium to the literary tradition, situating the book as a successor to John of Salisbury's Metalogicon.
Smith names concrete weaknesses: the absence of formal sentence analysis, a novel shorthand for categorical propositions, and rhetoric treated almost as an afterthought.
Despite intimidating density, Smith judges it perhaps the best single-volume resource for the arts of language, best suited to advanced college courses.
quotes: In recent years, many classical educators have made an effort to change the prevailing paradigm of the movement
the seven liberal arts (of which three encompass the Trivium: the arts of human order as expressed in language) are not incidental but central to any educational program
Joseph does not simply want to inform her reader about the Trivium: she wants to situate the reader within the liberal arts tradition
Joseph writes in a very compacted, almost scholastic prose that, like the process of reading Aristotle or Aquinas, requires the reader to pay great attention to every sentence
Despite its nature as a encyclopedic resource for the arts of language, The Trivium is ultimately a defense of the classical liberal arts for human flourishing.
if we want ourselves and our students to speak, write, and persuade others of reality at the highest level, The Trivium is perhaps the best available single-volume resource
